\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}

A world model predicts how observations change in response to actions. Recent work shows that
forecasting in the feature space of a frozen, self-supervised encoder such as DINOv2 or V-JEPA~2
gives compact models that support planning without generating pixels
\citep{zhou2025dinowm,assran2025vjepa2,maes2026lewm,sobal2025pldm}. These predictors are
\emph{generative in feature space}. At every future step they output the complete grid of patch
features, usually by feeding their own predictions back as inputs. In manipulation and surgical
video, however, most of the scene persists: tissue, tools, the table and the robot move, but they
are rarely created or destroyed. Regenerating persistent content at every step wastes capacity and
lets errors compound under recursion.

We ask a simple question. \emph{Can a latent world model forecast by transporting features it has
already observed, and synthesise only what transport cannot explain?} Motion-based video
prediction answered a version of this question in pixel space
\citep{finn2016advection,ebert2017skip,debrabandere2016dfn,liu2017voxelflow}. The idea has not been
tested for foundation-feature world models used for planning, where features are semantic,
high-dimensional and coarse in space. Three questions are open: whether transport helps once the
predictor is strong, whether it survives held-out real data, and what it costs for control.

We introduce \ours{} (\cref{fig:teaser,fig:method}). A memory encoder reads the patch features of
the last few observed frames. For each future step, a decoder conditioned on the causal
action-prefix state produces per-patch queries. Each query (i) attends to a local window of
\emph{observed} feature locations and copies their content, (ii) gates between staying in place and
moving, and (iii) adds a learned correction. Every horizon is predicted directly from measured
features, so errors do not compound through recursion, and the transport weights form a motion
field that we can inspect and compare against optical flow.

\paragraph{What is new.} \ours{} changes \emph{what} a latent world model predicts. Instead of regressing the
next feature grid, it predicts, for every future step, a motion of the grid it has already observed: a
per-patch transport over measured features, a gate and a residual. Three properties distinguish it from prior
work. (i) Unlike pixel-warping predictors \citep{finn2016advection,ebert2017skip,liu2017voxelflow}, it moves
\emph{semantic} foundation features that planners consume directly, and the move is conditioned on an explicit
action prefix. (ii) Unlike recursive latent world models \citep{zhou2025dinowm,maes2026lewm,assran2025vjepa2},
every horizon is computed directly from measured features, so errors cannot compound through feedback.
(iii) Its intermediate quantities---where each patch comes from, whether it moves, and what is new---are
explicit tensors that can be inspected and measured (\cref{fig:mechanism}).

\paragraph{Contributions.}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.2em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=2pt]
  \item \textbf{Method.} To our knowledge, \ours{} is the first latent world model that forecasts by
  action-conditioned transport of frozen foundation features. It is a drop-in output head for any frozen patch
  encoder and adds $<\!0.3\%$ parameters to a matched predictor.
  \item \textbf{Theory.} Under a motion model, the MSE-optimal forecast is a transport of observed features; additive
  heads must learn the feature contrast along the motion; recursive rollouts compound error (\cref{sec:theory}).
  \item \textbf{Held-out evidence.} Against predictors with the same backbone, \ours{} has the lowest held-out error on
  real robot video (DROID; \droidSkill\% vs.\ \droidSkillAR\% skill for recursive AR) and on seven surgical robot tasks,
  and we evaluate it on IWS, BridgeData V2, RT-1 and three planning suites.
  \item \textbf{Plug-in for published world models.} Added to V-JEPA 2-AC, the head lowers forecast error by
  \vjepaMSERed\% under an identical fine-tuning budget; added to DINO-WM with its official code, it changes latent
  prediction error by $-$\dinowmPushtErrRed\% (PushT) and $-$\dinowmWallErrRed\% (Wall) (\cref{sec:plugin}).
  \item \textbf{Mechanism.} We show that transport keeps forecasts sharp where regression blurs, that the learned
  field follows measured motion, and how an action-contrastive objective keeps anchored forecasts sensitive to
  actions for planning.
\end{itemize}
